newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada prepares to fight U.S. floodwaters.
newsitem.headline: Canada prepares to fight U.S. floodwaters.

text.p: The Canadian Armed Forces will deploy troops and equipment to battle what may be the highest Red River flood since the 1860s, a senior Canadian cabinet minister said Thursday.

"It's now a matter of providing the best protection we possibly can," Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy said as the Red River shattered 20th century records at Fargo, North Dakota, and was forecast to peak in Grand Forks Saturday.
The northward-flowing river, fed by a record winter snowfall in the Dakotas, should crest at the U.S.-Canadian border in a week and in Winnipeg April 29, forecasters said.

While the Canadian Armed Forces prepared the deployment, Canada Coast Guard had a fleet of small boats and equipment on alert for use by Manitoba municipalities and had mobilized several large barges to move livestock, Axworthy said.

Canada Customs said it was ready to permit the passage of emergency vehicles across the border if needed, Axworthy said. Officials were also in contact with Indian reservations on the Roseau and Dauphin rivers that are at risk of being isolated by rising water.
Radio updates were directing volunteers to sandbagging locations as temperatures in Winnipeg were forecast to reach a high of 6 Celsius (43 F) Thursday, leading to rapid snow melt.
"A lot of snow should melt so it could go up a foot in the next 24 hours," Winnipeg Harbour Master Joe Pietracci said.
The Red River at Winnipeg was 5.5 feet (1.7 metres) above the winter ice level Thursday and was forecast to exceed the century's record of 19 feet (5.8 metres) by month's end, Pietracci said.

High school students sandbagged riverfront property throughout Winnipeg to stave off the rising flood water. "I'm very proud of them but I'm sure they're going to feel it tomorrow," Maria Stewart-Docker said from her south end home.
About 275 square miles (712 square kilometres) flooded the last time the Red peaked April 20, 1996.

Manitoba Natural Resources has estimated there is a 50 percent chance of the worst flooding along the Red River in Canada since the 1860s, which could put more than 400 square miles (1,036 square kilometres) of farmland under water.
